To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the intestinal T cell population is immature at birth, but that the small and large intestine differ in the timing of appearance and phenotype of T cells that mature in the gut during the first 3 wk of postnatal life.
the appearance of intestinal T cell populations during suckling is different in the large and the small intestine and that the differences between these populations become established after weaning.
IEL in suckling mice are phenotypically different from IEL in adult animals and that these differences are more pronounced in the small than in the large intestines.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of T cells in the gut.
the development of the intestinal intraepithial lymphocytes (IELs) during the first three weeks after birth.
the development and function of the intestinal immune system, and we have identified a number of factors that contribute to differences in the intestinal immune system of mice.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the IEL population in the small intestine of the neonatal mouse is immature, and that this population matures during the first few weeks of life.
the gut is a very important organ during early postnatal development and that the immune system is a very important component of this organ.
the intestinal epithelium is an immunologically privileged site that is protected from the immune system.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the small intestine is the major site of IEL development and that T cell maturation in the gut is dependent upon the presence of TCR αβ and CD2.
TCR αβ and TCR γ δ IEL are phenotypically different in the large and the small intestine of adult mice, but not at birth.
IEL in neonatal mice are immature in comparison to IEL in adult animals.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the gut is not sterile, and the immune cells are not just passively acquired from the mother, but are actually developing in the gut.
